Vet of 11 years here. I respectfully disagree a bit on private equity. In places like Texas, it’s pushing independent clinics to sell or shut down, and it’s getting harder to find privately owned practices. They can outbid individual vets for clinics, and those higher buy-ins often lead to higher client costs.

Meanwhile, most vets and staff don’t directly benefit from those price increases unless they have equity. Compensation model can also influence vets behavior. Some vets, especially in high-volume settings, that could make more money may over recommend. Although this is not the norm. 

I always recommend what I believe is best for diagnosis and treatment, and most of us do the same.

This Doctor,  communicates thoughtfully, which I appreciate. Dr. Mike, it could be interesting to also hear from a vet willing to share stronger takes on topics like private equity, nutrition, and compensation.

Really enjoyed the conversation.

My grandfather had an overweight shitzu (40 pounds). The dog was extremely unhealthy as he solely fed it human fast food (McDonalds) because the dog "liked it" and he wanted it to be happy. The dog ended up tearing both hind suspensories and could not walk more than a few feet. This went on for years and he refused to take the dog to the vet, despite being hounded by family. Why? Because he was too cheap, despite being financially well-off. In his eyes the dog was healthy (because it was still breathing). Eventually at 10 years old the dog stopped eating, couldnt move at all, and was throwing up. After two days of this he finally agreed to take the dog to the vet. Before even receiving answers he already complained about the price. Turns out the poor dog had diabetes, liver failure, kidney disease, UTI, and the torn hind suspensories. The dog needed to be euthanized immediately. This dog only knew suffering, despite living in a nice house with a person who "loved" it. The dog never visited the vet or received any medical care it's entire life.

I strongly believe that majority of the people in this world should not own pets. Even if they have the financial means and the love and kind-handedness, it does not mean that they have the knowledge, values, or empathy to be able to properly care for an animal.

I have one clarifying comment for this video, other than this, I've been really happy to hear all the sides of this. 

There is a fundamental misunderstanding that keeps getting repeated through this video. It's not that the vets are getting paid by the companies or by recommending specific things, it's that the vet schools are funded by the companies for pet food and pharma companies, and have too much control over what vets are exposed to and educated on in schools. Therefore leading to vets that mean their best, but not having the picture outside of the approved curriculum. Similar to any indoctrination system that limits what you're exposed to without you truly knowing your knowledge was limited. 

That being said, I love that she's willing to support homemade food and seems to have gotten through this barrier, but a lot of vets do not get to the point of being willing to recommend anything but the companies known to fund vet education and will vilify anything else without even looking at it simply because it wasn't pushed as the correct food in school. There is a fine balance, and not every vet will do that walk and put in that time to look outside of what was required reading for passing schooling, but just like with everything else there are people who didn't fit that box. The concern is not for those vets, the concern and the complaint is for the system and for how hard it is to find those vets. 

Edit to add a configuring point. It's not that the companies need to pay for everything to have a big impact, just like when we look at the government and see the independent companies that chip in to problematic or mysterious projects. We look at what they're getting out of it as donors, and what specific strings they have or may have pulled to get specific things in front of specific audiences, though they will not touch the other aspects that don't benefit them.

comments.text:
Doctor Mike, thank you so much for having this conversation and putting this video out there. It's so important that people know the importance of portioning food correctly for our fur babies. I learned the hard way, because my beloved soul cat was free fed, (I was never told any differently, by vets or anyone, but still my fault for not doing the research.) He was fine for 11 years, but it was like he was getting chonky, and I saw him as my lil baby and just didn't see how much weight he gained over the years. He almost made it to his 12th birthday. 

He was always a lazy dude, but would still be playful sometimes, and never showed any signs of anything until it was too late. One day, he was perfectly fine. Overnight, he was suddenly very sluggish, he seemed weak in his back legs, he was peeing outside the litter box, wasn't eating much, etc. We took him to the vet and they did some tests, and they said he had kidney disease, and to give him special food. so we got the prescription food, and gave it to him. the next day, he was even worse. we took him back. they did more tests, and they said he was very sick. He was in diabetic ketoacidosis. We had to take him to a specialist center where he was hospitalized. We had to fundraise over $7k for the 4 days he was there, and we couldn't afford any more. So we asked what to do, and they said he was well enough to go home, but to just try to get him to eat, and give insulin shots, etc. we tried everything we could at home, he kept deteriorating, and was suffering. So we had to make the hard decision to take him back to the vet and I was like "just be real with me, is he going to get better, or is it better to stop his suffering" because I was so upset that he was suffering so much. They recommended the latter. So we had to say goodbye. 

If we had just portioned his food correctly, he could have lived another 5-10 years. It was a harrowing experience. I'll never make that mistake again. PSA: please don't free-feed your pets. Count their calories, watch their weight, feed high quality food.
